title: Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends
question: Why did rising transistor counts stop guaranteeing faster single-thread execution?
scope: Historical cross-chip observations with series-specific units on a logarithmic axis; the plot does not isolate a controlled causal intervention.

steps.title: Separate the quantities
steps.description: The legend assigns different units to transistor count, benchmark performance, frequency, power, and cores. Their vertical positions cannot be compared as if they were the same resource.

steps.title: Locate the architectural transition
steps.description: The gray band marks the end of broad Dennard scaling in the mid-2000s. It is a historical reference interval, not a measured discontinuity on every chip.

steps.title: Compare capacity with clock rate
steps.description: Red transistor points keep rising while green frequency points remain in a much narrower band. More transistors no longer translate into proportional clock increases.

steps.title: Look for parallel resources
steps.description: Logical core counts rise after staying near one in earlier decades. This motivates parallel execution and specialization rather than relying on faster sequential code.

title: Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard
question: Can a model pass the flash check and still miss its response deadline?
scope: This is the tightened 50 ms scorecard, not the canonical 200 ms scenario. Flash fit does not establish SRAM fit or complete-path latency.

steps.title: Read demand over supply
steps.description: The horizontal scale normalizes each demand by its own budget. The dashed line at 1 marks exact saturation, so bars beyond it fail that check.

steps.title: Pass the flash screen
steps.description: The short green Memory (flash) bar occupies only a small part of flash capacity. Runtime state and activations in SRAM remain separate checks.

steps.title: Miss the tightened deadline
steps.description: The red Latency (SLA) bar reaches 202 percent of the 50 ms budget. A model can fit its stored weights yet still respond too slowly.

steps.title: Identify the actual binding check
steps.description: In this tightened case latency fails while flash passes. Changing the deadline changes that verdict without shrinking the model or accelerating execution.

title: Dynamic Graph Execution Flow
question: Why does eager execution expose only one Python call at a time?
scope: The GPU box denotes dispatch of device work; asynchronous execution does not imply Python waits for kernel completion.

steps.title: Encounter a call
steps.description: Python reaches Define Operation and asks the framework to issue the corresponding work. This makes the current operation directly inspectable.

steps.title: Dispatch device work
steps.description: The runtime enqueues the GPU operation. The device may execute asynchronously while the host continues; the drawing is not a synchronization barrier.

steps.title: Return for another call
steps.description: The Yes branch returns to Python for the next operation. That boundary limits visibility into future Python calls and opportunities for optimization across them.

steps.title: Finish the sequence
steps.description: The No branch ends this sequence of calls. Completion of host dispatch and completion of asynchronous device work remain distinct events.

steps.title: Submit a captured region

title: The Compilation Continuum
question: When can repeated execution repay compilation cost?
scope: Illustrative arbitrary-unit model, not a measured benchmark or a forecast for a particular model.

steps.title: Pay once before reuse
steps.description: JIT and AOT start above eager because their one-time compilation cost is nonzero. Their lower execution cost matters only after enough reuse.

steps.title: Prefer eager at low counts
steps.description: The blue eager curve is lowest in the broad left region. Avoiding compilation wins while the program runs too few times to repay the upfront work.

steps.title: Cross into JIT
steps.description: Near the first dotted boundary, the orange JIT curve falls below eager in total cost. The horizontal axis is logarithmic, so equal spacing does not mean equal additional executions.

steps.title: Amortize the larger AOT cost
steps.description: At the right boundary, the green AOT curve becomes lowest. Changing compilation or execution costs moves both crossover points.

title: Sparse Matrix Transformation
question: What does magnitude pruning change before any sparse kernel runs?
scope: This example illustrates a mask over weight values. Zero entries in an unchanged dense allocation do not by themselves reduce allocated bytes or runtime.

steps.title: Inspect magnitudes
steps.description: The left matrix mixes small values with larger positive and negative weights. Magnitude-based pruning compares absolute values rather than pruning by sign.

steps.title: Replace selected values with zeros
steps.description: The right matrix preserves its grid while many cells become white zero entries. The numerical mask changes values, not automatically the allocation shape.

steps.title: Retain important candidates
steps.description: Larger-magnitude entries remain colored, including negative weights. Magnitude is a pruning heuristic, so task-quality recovery and validation still matter.

steps.title: Require an execution representation
steps.description: Sparse storage and a matching kernel can turn these zeros into skipped data and work. A dense kernel may still read and multiply the full grid.

title: Channel vs. Layer Pruning

steps.title: Bypass a complete stage
steps.description: Layer pruning removes all channels in one stage and rewires the graph. Remaining stages must accept the new interfaces and recover the removed function.

steps.title: Profile the rewritten model

title: Low-Rank Factorization
question: When can two factors represent a weight matrix with fewer parameters?
scope: W is approximated by U times V-transpose. Lower storage requires k(m+n) to be below mn, and accuracy and runtime must be validated.

w.label: Original m by n matrix W

u.label: Left m by k factor U

vt.label: Right k by n factor V transpose

steps.title: Count the original representation
steps.description: W contains m times n stored values. Its full dense operation provides the reference against which compression is evaluated.

steps.title: Introduce the shared rank
steps.description: U has shape m by k and V-transpose has shape k by n. The shared dimension k makes their product compatible with W.

steps.title: Trade one operation for two
steps.description: The factors store k(m+n) values and execute two factor operations. Choosing a small k may save storage but introduces approximation error and additional kernel boundaries.

title: Tensor Decomposition
question: How do three mode-specific factors reconstruct one tensor entry?
scope: This is a low-rank approximation. The highlighted vectors identify one entry; the image does not guarantee a particular accuracy or speedup.

title: Soft Target Distribution

steps.title: Use a richer training signal

title: Knowledge Distillation Workflow
question: Why does student training need both soft and hard supervision paths?

steps.title: Share the example
steps.description: Input x feeds both networks. The teacher supplies a target distribution while the smaller student produces predictions for training.

steps.title: Match softened predictions
steps.description: The teacher's soft labels and the student's soft predictions use temperature greater than 1. Distillation loss compares these distributions.

steps.title: Retain task supervision
steps.description: The student also produces predictions at temperature 1. Student loss compares them against the ground-truth hard label rather than the teacher distribution.

steps.title: Deploy the trained student

title: Neural Architecture Search Flow
question: How does architecture search use evaluation feedback?
scope: Search quality depends on its defined space, estimator, and resource bounds. The feedback loop does not guarantee a globally optimal architecture.

steps.title: Define the allowable designs
steps.description: Search Space determines which architectures can be proposed. A useful hardware-efficient design outside this space cannot be discovered by the loop.

steps.title: Propose a candidate
steps.description: Search Strategy selects an architecture from that space and sends it to evaluation. The proposal is a model structure, not an already validated deployment.

steps.title: Evaluate the target requirements
steps.description: Performance Estimation assesses candidate quality and relevant hardware constraints. Measured or estimated latency can differ from a simple FLOP count.

steps.title: Use feedback for the next proposal
steps.description: The return arrow carries the performance estimate to the strategy. Search spends evaluation resources to steer later candidates toward the desired trade-off.

title: Early Exit Architecture
question: When can an input stop before the final transformer layer?
scope: This is an architecture walkthrough, not a calibrated confidence simulator. Batched execution may require compaction or otherwise fail to realize proportional savings.

steps.title: Compute an intermediate representation
steps.description: Transformer 1 processes the input before Classifier 1 forms an early prediction. The extra classifier and estimator themselves incur work.

steps.title: Test the exit policy
steps.description: Confidence/LTE determines whether the intermediate prediction meets the exit criterion. Confidence must be calibrated and validated for the task.

steps.title: Stop or continue
steps.description: A permitted Exit skips remaining transformer stages for that input. Otherwise the Continue path sends its representation onward.

steps.title: Separate skipped work from speedup
steps.description: Later stages remain available for harder inputs. Savings in a batch depend on how the runtime handles examples that exit at different depths.

title: Switch Transformer Architecture
question: How does sparse expert routing separate total parameters from per-token work?
scope: The diagram shows top-1 routing for two example tokens. Unselected experts can remain resident in memory; routing overhead and imbalance still matter.

steps.title: Replace the dense FFN stage
steps.description: The left block places Switching FFN between the transformer's attention and normalization stages. The right panel expands this one stage.

steps.title: Route each token
steps.description: The More and Parameters tokens reach routers that select one expert each. Different tokens can take different expert paths.

steps.title: Execute only the selected expert
steps.description: The shown routes choose FFN 2 for one token and FFN 1 for the other. The full expert bank increases model capacity without executing every expert for every token.

steps.title: Keep the systems cost visible
steps.description: The expert output is weighted and returned to the transformer path. All-resident expert weights still consume memory, and uneven routing can leave some experts overloaded and others idle.

title: Illustrative Quantization Regimes
question: Why must a low-bit deployment validate the accuracy cliff for its own model?
scope: The two named curves are illustrative assumed regimes, not measured ResNet-50 or BERT benchmarks. Breakpoints are not general precision recommendations.

steps.title: Read precision in the plotted direction
steps.description: The axis runs from FP32 on the left toward fewer bits on the right. This is a precision choice, not training time.

steps.title: Inspect the assumed plateau
steps.description: Both curves stay relatively flat over part of the range. This illustrates tolerance to some quantization error, not a guarantee of lossless conversion.

steps.title: Locate the model-dependent cliff
steps.description: At the narrowest formats the illustrative curves fall sharply and differently. Calibration, outliers, quantizer design, and task evaluation determine the actual boundary.

steps.title: Treat the labels as scenarios
steps.description: The legend names example model families, but the plotted values are stipulated. A deployment decision requires quality measurements for the actual model and execution path.

title: Floating-Point Bit Layouts
question: Why do FP16 and BF16 spend the same storage budget differently?
scope: The drawing compares bit layouts, not measured compute speed. Exponent range and fraction precision have different effects.

steps.title: Establish the FP32 baseline
steps.description: FP32 allocates one sign bit, eight exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. Exponent and fraction serve different purposes: range and significand resolution.

steps.title: Spend more FP16 bits on the fraction
steps.description: FP16 uses five exponent bits and ten fraction bits. Its narrower exponent range can make small training updates underflow, motivating loss scaling.

steps.title: Preserve exponent range in BF16
steps.description: BF16 retains eight exponent bits but only seven fraction bits. It preserves a range similar to FP32 while sacrificing significand precision.

steps.title: Separate storage from arithmetic behavior
steps.description: Both 16-bit formats halve raw value storage relative to FP32. Their different layouts still require appropriate numerical and hardware support.

review_notes: Visually inspected canonical rendered artwork and checked local QMD context; original geometry and labels retained.

title: Quantization Engineering Workflow
question: When should frozen-weight calibration give way to training or custom execution?
scope: The tiers order engineering effort rather than guaranteeing quality. INT8, INT4, per-channel scaling, and mixed precision can appear across stages.

steps.title: Try calibration without retraining
steps.description: Post-Training (PTQ) starts with frozen pretrained weights. It avoids gradient updates but still requires representative calibration and task validation.

steps.title: Recover quality through training
steps.description: Quantization-Aware (QAT) introduces simulated noise while fine-tuning floating-point weights. It spends training compute when the frozen-weight candidate falls short.

steps.title: Require a matching datapath
steps.description: Specialized & Extreme formats may need custom kernels and hardware co-design. A narrower representation is useful only with supported execution and validated quality.

title: Illustrative Aggregate Quantization Residuals
question: What distinguishes bounded rounding error from larger aggregate residual tails?
scope: Illustrative aggregate residual density, not one uniform quantizer with a declared scale. The horizontal values are not a universal half-step bound.

steps.title: Locate the typical residual
steps.description: The tallest bars cluster near zero. Quantization changes values even when most differences remain small.

steps.title: Inspect both tails
steps.description: The red callouts draw attention to larger negative and positive residuals. Rare larger errors can matter even when the distribution is centered.

steps.title: Keep the quantizer boundary explicit
steps.description: For one unclipped uniform quantizer, nearest rounding stays within half a step. These aggregate tails instead represent clipping or a mixture of step sizes, so the displayed axis does not define that bound.

title: Post-Training Quantization Pipeline
question: What does calibration learn when pretrained weights stay frozen?
scope: This PTQ workflow does not retrain weights. Calibration quality and supported integer execution must be validated before deployment.

steps.title: Start from a trained model
steps.description: The pretrained model enters with its learned floating-point weights. PTQ avoids a new gradient-training phase.

steps.title: Observe representative activation ranges
steps.description: Calibration data passes through the model so the calibration stage can estimate ranges and associated scale and zero-point metadata. Unrepresentative data can miss deployment tails.

steps.title: Convert the representation
steps.description: Quantization maps weights and supported activation boundaries to lower precision using the chosen metadata. Calibration itself has not adapted the model weights.

steps.title: Validate the exported candidate
steps.description: The quantized model is a deployment candidate. Check task quality and the real kernel path; a frozen-weight conversion can require revised ranges, granularity, or QAT.

title: Activation Distribution
question: Why can a long activation tail waste integer resolution?
scope: The marked boundary near 1.1 is a candidate, not an identified percentile. Choosing it requires cumulative counts and task validation.

steps.title: Inspect the dense bulk
steps.description: The tallest bars sit near small activation values. Allocating most integer levels to this populated range can improve resolution.

steps.title: Find the long tail
steps.description: A sparse tail extends beyond the bulk. Keeping its full span consumes part of a fixed integer grid even where few activation values occur.

steps.title: Test a candidate boundary
steps.description: The dashed threshold proposes clipping near the end of the bulk. Clipping can distort rare but important cases, so its apparent visual convenience is not enough.

steps.title: Validate rather than infer a percentile
steps.description: The axis shows activation magnitude, not cumulative frequency. The diagram does not establish which percentile the candidate boundary represents.

title: Calibration Range Selection
question: How does an affine zero-point preserve real zero in a non-centered range?
scope: Printed ranges illustrate symmetric and asymmetric affine maps. Rounding conventions and saturation must still match the deployed kernel.

realzero.label: Real zero maps to integer z

integerzero.label: Integer zero has a shifted real coordinate

steps.title: Use equal-magnitude bounds
steps.description: The left mapping spans real values from -1 to 1 and integer values from -127 to 127. Real zero maps to integer zero in the symmetric case.

steps.title: Shift the represented interval
steps.description: The right mapping spans real values from -0.5 to 1.5. A generally nonzero zero-point lets a single scale represent this non-centered interval.

steps.title: Preserve exact zero
steps.description: The green real-zero marker maps to the integer z marker. Integer zero therefore need not correspond to real zero in the asymmetric map.

title: Quantization Range Variation
question: Why can one layerwide range underserve narrow channels?
scope: The distributions are schematic. Per-channel scales add metadata and require supported kernels; the figure is not a measured accuracy comparison.

steps.title: Separate the filters
steps.description: The selected layer expands into filters 1 through C. Their weight distributions have different widths.

steps.title: Share one range
steps.description: The Layerwise Quantization column uses common red bounds. A range wide enough for the broadest filter leaves fewer effective levels across a narrow filter's values.

steps.title: Fit each channel locally
steps.description: The Channelwise Quantization column adapts blue bounds to each distribution. Local ranges can preserve resolution at the cost of additional scale metadata and execution complexity.

steps.title: Validate the complete format
steps.description: Per-channel ranges are a representation choice, not a guarantee of faster inference. Metadata, packing, arithmetic, and kernel support must fit the deployment.

title: Quantized Matrix Multiplication Pipeline
question: Why does INT8 matrix multiplication still need an INT32 accumulation stage?
scope: The two floating inputs represent operands. This schematic omits implementation details such as bias handling and assumes supported affine integer execution.

steps.title: Quantize both operands
steps.description: The two input paths convert floating-point values to INT8. Their scale and zero-point metadata define how these integers represent real values.

steps.title: Accumulate with room for sums
steps.description: Matrix Multiplication consumes INT8 operands, but the sum of many products needs a wider INT32 accumulator. Low-precision inputs do not imply an 8-bit running sum.

steps.title: Rescale before the next layer
steps.description: Requantization maps the accumulated result back to the intended output scale and clips to the INT8 range. This is a numerical transformation, not merely dropping high bits.

steps.title: Apply the supported activation path
steps.description: Activation follows the rescaled values and produces INT8 Output in this diagram. The deployed kernel must preserve the intended scales and nonlinear behavior.

title: Quantization-Aware Training Pipeline
question: How can training adapt weights to the errors of quantized inference?
scope: The flowchart abstracts fake quantization and STE. It does not mean that master weights or gradient updates are stored and optimized entirely as INT8.

steps.title: Begin with pretrained weights
steps.description: The model supplies a learned floating-point starting point. Quantization-aware training adds the deployment precision constraints to the training procedure.

steps.title: Simulate rounding and clipping
steps.description: The quantization stage represents fake quantization in the forward graph. It exposes the model to the numerical distortion expected at deployment.

steps.title: Update floating-point parameters
steps.description: Training data drives Retraining/Finetuning. Approximate STE gradients pass through the rounding operation so floating-point master weights can adapt.

steps.title: Export and validate inference
steps.description: The final Quantized model uses the chosen integer representation and scales. Training adaptation has a compute cost and does not remove the need for deployment quality checks.

title: PTQ-to-QAT Pipeline
question: Why can calibration data initialize a later QAT training phase?
scope: This is one candidate workflow, not a requirement for every quantized deployment. Calibration data and gradient-training data have distinct roles.

steps.title: Initialize from a trained model
steps.description: The pretrained model enters the PTQ group. Its learned weights provide the starting behavior for calibration.

steps.title: Estimate ranges without gradients
steps.description: Calibrate data feeds Calibrate model in PTQ. The resulting ranges and scales initialize the lower-precision candidate while weights remain frozen in this phase.

steps.title: Adapt with training data
steps.description: The PTQ model enters the QAT group. Training data now drives Fine-tune model with simulated quantization and floating-point weight updates.

steps.title: Export the adapted candidate
steps.description: The QAT model is the result of the training phase. It must still satisfy quality thresholds and supported target execution.

title: Illustrative Layer-Wise Sparsity Distribution
question: Does a darker layer necessarily execute faster?
scope: This mixed-layer schematic is not a measurement from one trained model. Zero density alone establishes neither redundancy nor runtime benefit.

steps.title: Decode the shade
steps.description: The legend maps darker tiles to higher zero density. Shade counts removed weights in this schematic; it is not a time or bandwidth scale.

steps.title: Compare layer families
steps.description: The convolutional rows show lighter shades while the fully connected rows are darker. This illustrates a nonuniform policy, not verified redundancy in all fully connected layers.

steps.title: Keep transformer components distinct
steps.description: Attention and MLP rows have their own patterns. Different tensors can use different layouts and kernels even when their zero density is similar.

steps.title: Profile the usable representation
steps.description: To claim savings, pair each row's density with a sparse storage format and supported kernel profile. Dense execution may still process every zero.
